# 2 Kings Chapter 22 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 243r–243v

---

**1** Josiah was eight years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for thirty-one years. His mother was Jedidah daughter of Adaiah from Bozkath.

**2** He did what was right in the LORD's sight. He followed the example of his ancestor David completely, never deviating from it.

**3** In the eighteenth year of his reign, King Josiah sent his secretary Shaphan son of Azaliah, grandson of Meshullam, to the LORD's temple with these instructions:

**4** "Go to the high priest Hilkiah and have him count the money the people have donated to the temple — the funds collected by the doorkeepers.

**5** Have them turn it over to the supervisors of the temple restoration, who can then pay the workers repairing the LORD's temple —

**6** the carpenters, builders, and masons — and use it to purchase timber and cut stone for the repairs."

**7** No audit of the funds was required, because the workers were completely honest.

**8** Then Hilkiah the high priest told Shaphan the secretary, "I have found the Book of the Law in the LORD's temple!" He handed the scroll to Shaphan, who read it.

**9** Shaphan went to the king and reported, "Your officials have paid out the money from the temple and turned it over to the restoration supervisors."

**10** Then Shaphan added, "Hilkiah the priest gave me a book." And Shaphan read it aloud to the king.

**11** When the king heard what was written in the Book of the Law, he tore his robes in anguish.

**12** He immediately gave orders to Hilkiah the priest, Ahikam son of Shaphan, Achbor son of Micaiah, Shaphan the secretary, and Asaiah the king's attendant:

**13** "Go and consult the LORD on my behalf and on behalf of all the people of Judah about what is written in this book that has been found. The LORD's fury must be burning against us, because our ancestors did not obey what this book says — they failed to follow everything written in it about us."

**14** So Hilkiah the priest, along with Ahikam, Achbor, Shaphan, and Asaiah, went to see Huldah the prophetess. She was the wife of Shallum son of Tikvah, grandson of Harhas, who was in charge of the temple wardrobe. She lived in Jerusalem's Second Quarter. They laid the matter before her.

**15** She told them, "This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: Tell the man who sent you to me,

**16** 'This is what the LORD says: I am going to bring disaster on this place and its people — everything written in the book the king of Judah has read.

**17** Because they have abandoned me and burned incense to other gods, provoking me with everything they have done, my anger will burn against this place and will not be quenched.'

**18** But say this to the king of Judah, who sent you to seek the LORD's will: 'This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says about the words you have heard:

**19** Because your heart was responsive and you humbled yourself before the LORD when you heard what I declared against this place and its people — that they would become an object of horror and a curse — and because you tore your robes and wept before me, I have heard you,' declares the LORD.

**20** 'Therefore I will let you die in peace and be buried with your ancestors. You will not see the disaster I am going to bring on this place.'" They reported her words to the king.

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**Verse 8 — "The Book of the Law":** This is one of the most consequential moments in biblical history. The scroll discovered during temple renovations is almost certainly a version of Deuteronomy. Its rediscovery launches the most sweeping religious reform in Judah's history — and raises the troubling question of how the nation's foundational document could have been lost in the first place.

**Verse 11 — Josiah tears his robes:** The king's response is immediate, visceral, and without self-justification. He reads (or hears read) the covenant demands and the curses for disobedience, recognizes that Judah stands condemned, and reacts with genuine grief. This is the opposite of Manasseh's indifference.

**Verse 14 — Huldah the prophetess:** Both Jeremiah and Zephaniah are active prophets at this time. Yet the king's delegation goes to Huldah — a woman — without any hint that this is unusual. Her oracle is authoritative, two-layered, and devastating: the nation is doomed (vv.16-17), but the king personally will be spared witnessing the destruction (vv.19-20).

**Verse 20 — "die in peace":** A puzzling promise, since Josiah dies in battle (23:29). "Peace" here seems to mean that he dies before Jerusalem falls — he is spared the worst, even if his own death is violent.

*— PNEUMA*
